query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a high‐entropy alloy initially engineered as a single-phase solid solution, exposure to the high‐stress and high‐temperature conditions of demanding service induces local compositional fluctuations that trigger phase decomposition. This decomposition results in the nucleation and growth of brittle secondary phases (for example, intermetallic or Laves phases) preferentially at grain boundaries, which in turn act as sites for crack initiation and propagation under mechanical loading, thereby resulting in a loss of toughness and a transition to brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) as produced by rapid solidification or other advanced processing methods yielding uniform body‐centered cubic (BCC) or similar solid solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject specimens to a controlled thermal or stress aging treatment designed to simulate harsh engineering service (e.g., elevated temperatures combined with sustained or cyclic mechanical loading) that is expected to promote phase decomposition and precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: Test conditions replicate the demanding service environment, for example, high temperature (potentially ≥500°C, depending on alloy specifics) combined with high mechanical stress levels or cyclic loading that challenge the intrinsic ductility of the material.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and precipitation of brittle secondary phases (such as Laves phases or other intermetallic compounds) along grain boundaries or within the matrix, which serve as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites.
generation.mechanism: Thermal or stress exposure leads to local compositional inhomogeneities that lower the stability of the original single-phase structure, permitting the nucleation and growth of brittle precipitates. These precipitates reduce the alloy’s capacity to absorb energy during deformation, thereby decreasing toughness and promoting brittle fracture under load.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast, single-phase baseline, the thermally or stress-aged specimens will exhibit a measurable reduction in toughness (e.g., reduced Charpy impact energy and lower crack propagation resistance), increased microhardness (due to the brittle precipitates), and fracture surfaces characteristic of brittle failure (cleavage facets, intergranular fracture features).
generation.baseline: The unaged, as-cast HEA exhibiting a uniform, ductile single-phase microstructure with no detectable brittle secondary phases.
generation.boundary: The effect is anticipated to occur under service conditions combining elevated temperatures and mechanical loads approaching or exceeding the alloy’s yield strength. Service boundaries include high-temperature structural applications where sustained or cyclic stresses are present.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nature, volume fraction, and distribution of the brittle phases, as well as the quantitative reduction in toughness, may vary with the specific alloy composition and processing history. The threshold temperature and stress levels required to trigger phase decomposition are also somewhat uncertain and warrant further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same high-entropy alloy batch, ensuring an identical, single-phase microstructure in the as-cast state. Subject one set to a controlled thermal (and/or mechanical) aging treatment designed to promote phase decomposition under conditions simulating demanding service (e.g., exposure at elevated temperatures and cyclic loading). Retain the other set as the baseline without aging. Perform mechanical testing (tensile, Charpy impact) to assess toughness, complemented by microstructural analysis (XRD, SEM/EDS) to detect the presence and distribution of any brittle phases.
measurements: Charpy impact energy and/or fracture toughness values
Phase identification by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy (SEM, TEM) to identify brittle precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in toughness (i.e., similar impact energy, fracture toughness, and ductile fracture morphology) or if no evidence of brittle secondary phase formation is detected compared to the baseline single-phase material, then the hypothesis that phase decomposition leads to decreased toughness and brittle fracture under mechanical loading will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
